// Params ---------------------------------------------------------------------
struct Params {

  int device;
  int n_gpu_threads;
  int n_gpu_blocks;
  int n_warmup;
  int n_reps;
  int m;
  int n;
  int s;

  Params(int argc, char **argv) {
    device        = 0;
    n_gpu_threads  = 64;
    n_gpu_blocks = 16;
    n_warmup      = 10;
    n_reps        = 100;
    m             = 197;
    n             = 35588;
    s             = 32;
    int opt;
    while((opt = getopt(argc, argv, "hd:i:g:w:r:m:n:s:")) >= 0) {
      switch(opt) {
        case 'h':
          usage();
          exit(0);
          break;
        case 'i': n_gpu_threads  = atoi(optarg); break;
        case 'g': n_gpu_blocks = atoi(optarg); break;
        case 'w': n_warmup      = atoi(optarg); break;
        case 'r': n_reps        = atoi(optarg); break;
        case 'm': m             = atoi(optarg); break;
        case 'n': n             = atoi(optarg); break;
        case 's': s             = atoi(optarg); break;
        default:
            fprintf(stderr, "\nUnrecognized option!\n");
            usage();
            exit(0);
      }
    }
  }

  void usage() {
    fprintf(stderr,
        "\nUsage:  ./main [options]"
        "\n"
        "\nGeneral options:"
        "\n    -h        help"
        "\n    -i <I>    # of device threads per block (default=64)"
        "\n    -g <G>    # of device blocks (default=16)"
        "\n    -w <W>    # of warmup iterations (default=10)"
        "\n    -r <R>    # of repetition iterations (default=100)"
        "\n"
        "\nBenchmark-specific options:"
        "\n    -m <M>    matrix height (default=197)"
        "\n    -n <N>    matrix width (default=35588)"
        "\n    -s <M>    super-element size (default=32)"
        "\n");
  }
};

// Input Data -----------------------------------------------------------------
void read_input(FP *x_vector, const Params &p) {
  int tiled_n = divceil(p.n, p.s);
  int in_size = p.m * tiled_n * p.s;
  srand(5432);
  for(int i = 0; i < in_size; i++) {
    x_vector[i] = ((FP)(rand() % 100) / 100);
  }
}

// Main ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
int main(int argc, char **argv) {

  const Params p(argc, argv);
  int blocks = p.n_gpu_blocks;
  int threads = p.n_gpu_threads;
  const int max_gpu_threads = 256;
  assert(threads <= max_gpu_threads && 
          "The thread block size is greater than the maximum thread block size that can be used on this device");


  // Allocate
  int tiled_n       = divceil(p.n, p.s);
  int in_size       = p.m * tiled_n * p.s;
  int finished_size = p.m * tiled_n;

  size_t in_size_bytes = in_size * sizeof(FP);
  size_t finished_size_bytes = finished_size * sizeof(int);

  FP *h_in_out = (FP *)malloc(in_size_bytes);
  int *h_finished = (int *)malloc(finished_size_bytes);
  int *h_head = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
  FP *h_in_backup = (FP *)malloc(in_size_bytes);

  // Initialize
  read_input(h_in_out, p);
  memcpy(h_in_backup, h_in_out, in_size_bytes); // Backup for reuse across iterations

  const int A = p.m;
  const int B = tiled_n;
  const int b = p.s;

#pragma omp target data map(alloc: h_in_out[0:in_size], \
                                   h_finished[0:finished_size], \
                                   h_head[0:1])
  {
    double time = 0;

    for(int rep = 0; rep < p.n_warmup + p.n_reps; rep++) {

      memcpy(h_in_out, h_in_backup, in_size_bytes);
      memset((void *)h_finished, 0, finished_size_bytes);
      h_head[0] = 0;

#pragma omp target update to(h_in_out[0:in_size]) // nowait
#pragma omp target update to(h_finished[0:finished_size]) // nowait
#pragma omp target update to(h_head[0:1]) // nowait

     auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

#pragma omp target teams num_teams(blocks) thread_limit(threads) 
      {
        int lmem[2];
#pragma omp parallel 
        {
          const int tid = omp_get_thread_num();
          int       m   = A * B - 1;

          if(tid == 0) {// Dynamic fetch
#pragma omp atomic capture
            lmem[1] = h_head[0]++;
          }
#pragma omp barrier

          while(lmem[1] < m) {
            int next_in_cycle = (lmem[1] * A) - m * (lmem[1] / B);
            if(next_in_cycle == lmem[1]) {
              if(tid == 0) {// Dynamic fetch
#pragma omp atomic capture
                lmem[1] = h_head[0]++;
              }
#pragma omp barrier
              continue;
            }
            FP   data1, data2, data3, data4;
            int i = tid;
            if(i < b)
              data1 = h_in_out[lmem[1] * b + i];
            i += omp_get_num_threads();
            if(i < b)
              data2 = h_in_out[lmem[1] * b + i];
            i += omp_get_num_threads();
            if(i < b)
              data3 = h_in_out[lmem[1] * b + i];
            i += omp_get_num_threads();
            if(i < b)
              data4 = omp_get_num_threads();

            if(tid == 0) {
#pragma omp atomic read
              lmem[0] = h_finished[lmem[1]];
            }
#pragma omp barrier

            for(; lmem[0] == 0; next_in_cycle = (next_in_cycle * A) - m * (next_in_cycle / B)) {
              FP backup1, backup2, backup3, backup4;
              i = tid;
              if(i < b)
                backup1 = h_in_out[next_in_cycle * b + i];
              i += omp_get_num_threads();
              if(i < b)
                backup2 = h_in_out[next_in_cycle * b + i];
              i += omp_get_num_threads();
              if(i < b)
                backup3 = h_in_out[next_in_cycle * b + i];
              i += omp_get_num_threads();
              if(i < b)
                backup4 = h_in_out[next_in_cycle * b + i];

              if(tid == 0) {
#pragma omp atomic capture
                {
                  lmem[0] = h_finished[next_in_cycle];
                  h_finished[next_in_cycle] = (int)1;
                }
              }
#pragma omp barrier

              if(!lmem[0]) {
                i = tid;
                if(i < b)
                  h_in_out[next_in_cycle * b + i] = data1;
                i += omp_get_num_threads();
                if(i < b)
                  h_in_out[next_in_cycle * b + i] = data2;
                i += omp_get_num_threads();
                if(i < b)
                  h_in_out[next_in_cycle * b + i] = data3;
                i += omp_get_num_threads();
                if(i < b)
                  h_in_out[next_in_cycle * b + i] = data4;
              }
              i = tid;
              if(i < b)
                data1 = backup1;
              i += omp_get_num_threads();
              if(i < b)
                data2 = backup2;
              i += omp_get_num_threads();
              if(i < b)
                data3 = backup3;
              i += omp_get_num_threads();
              if(i < b)
                data4 = backup4;
            }

            if(tid == 0) { // Dynamic fetch
#pragma omp atomic capture
              lmem[1] = h_head[0]++;
            }
#pragma omp barrier
          }

#include <cmath>
#include <stdio.h>

inline int compare_output(FP *output, FP *ref, int dim) {
    int i;
    int fail = 0;
    for(i = 0; i < dim; i++) {
        FP diff = fabs(ref[i] - output[i]);
        if((diff - 0.0f) > 0.00001f && diff > 0.01 * fabs(ref[i])) {
            printf("Failed at line: %d ref: %f actual: %f diff: %f\n", i, ref[i], output[i], diff);
            fail = 1;
	    break;
        }
    }
    return fail;
}

// Sequential transposition for comparison purposes
//[w][h/t][t] to [h/t][w][t]
inline void cpu_soa_asta(FP *src, FP *dst, int height, int width, int tile_size) {
    // We only support height == multiple of tile size
    if((height / tile_size) * tile_size == height)
        for(int k = 0; k < width; k++) {
            for(int i = 0; i < height / tile_size; i++) { //For all tiles
                for(int j = 0; j < tile_size; j++) {
                    //from src[k][i][j] to dst[i][k][j]
                    dst[i * width * tile_size + k * tile_size + j] = src[k * height + i * tile_size + j];
                }
            }
        }
}

inline int verify(FP *input2, FP *input, int height, int width, int tile_size) {
    FP *output = (FP *)malloc(width * height * sizeof(FP));
    cpu_soa_asta(input, output, height, width, tile_size);
    int status = compare_output(input2, output, height * width);
    free(output);
    return status;
}

prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: This kernel performs an in-place matrix transposition using a cycle-following algorithm. The data type FP is float (single precision, since DOUBLE_PRECISION is not defined). However, the kernel does NOT perform arithmetic floating-point operations on the data — it only reads, copies, and writes float values. The integer arithmetic (computing next_in_cycle, index calculations) does not count as FP32 FLOPs. There are no floating-point adds, multiplies, or other FP operations in the kernel. The only FP operations are loads and stores (assignments), which are not FLOPs. Therefore FP32 FLOP count is 0.

prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: No half-precision floating point operations are performed in this kernel. The kernel is a data transposition kernel that only moves float data without performing FP16 arithmetic.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Let me trace the parameters: A=197 (m), tiled_n = divceil(35588, 32) = ceil(35588/32) = 1113, B=1113, b=32. m (in kernel) = A*B - 1 = 197*1113 - 1 = 219260. The kernel performs an in-place permutation via cycle-following. Each element index from 0 to m-1 (219260 values) is visited. Each "element" is a super-element of size b=32 floats = 128 bytes. The h_in_out array has in_size = 197 * 1113 * 32 = 7,016,352 floats = ~28,065,408 bytes (~26.8 MB). The h_finished array has finished_size = 197 * 1113 = 219,261 ints = ~877,044 bytes (~0.84 MB). h_head is 4 bytes. Total unique read footprint: h_in_out (~28 MB) + h_finished (~0.88 MB) + h_head (4 bytes) ≈ 28.9 MB. The L2 cache is 6 MB, so the working set far exceeds L2. For h_in_out, each super-element is read once during cycle traversal (128 bytes each), and the total is about 219,261 * 128 = ~28 MB. For h_finished, each entry is read atomically, about 219,261 * 4 = ~0.88 MB. With 16 blocks and 64 threads, threads=1024 total. The reads from h_in_out: each thread reads up to 4 floats per super-element (with b=32, threads=64, so 32/64 < 1, meaning only tid < 32 reads, so ~32 floats = 128 bytes per work item). Total DRAM reads ≈ 28 MB + 0.88 MB ≈ 28.9 MB. Given cache thrashing with the large working set, DRAM reads approximate the unique footprint.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes to h_in_out (the transposed data), h_finished (marking elements as done), and h_head (atomic counter). For h_in_out: each super-element is written once during the permutation cycle, so ~219,261 super-elements * 128 bytes = ~28,065,408 bytes. For h_finished: each entry is written once (set to 1) via atomic, ~219,261 * 4 = ~877,044 bytes. For h_head: incremented atomically ~219,261 times but it's just 4 bytes (one cache line). Total unique write footprint ≈ 28 MB + 0.88 MB ≈ 28.9 MB. Since the working set (~29 MB) far exceeds the 6 MB L2 cache, most writes will be evicted to DRAM during the kernel execution. For h_finished, ~877,044 bytes are written (each element set to 1 once). h_head is incremented atomically ~219,261 times but is only 4 bytes. Total unique write footprint ≈ 28.9 MB, which exceeds the 6 MB L2 cache. Since writes are scattered following permutation cycles, cache line evictions will push most writes to DRAM. The write traffic to DRAM ≈ 28,061,568 (h_in_out) + 877,044 (h_finished) + 128 (h_head cache line) ≈ 28,938,740 bytes. With write-allocate behavior for scattered writes, there may be some amplification, but the unique footprint is the baseline.

metrics_explanations.gridSz_explanation: The kernel is launched with `num_teams(blocks)` where blocks = p.n_gpu_blocks = 16. The OpenMP runtime for clang targeting NVIDIA GPUs typically adds one extra warp for the "master" thread management, so the actual block count launched is 16 teams. The grid is 1D, so gridSz = [16, 1, 1].
metrics_explanations.blockSz_explanation: The kernel uses `thread_limit(threads)` where threads = p.n_gpu_threads = 64. The LLVM OpenMP runtime for GPU typically adds one extra warp (32 threads) for the "generic" execution mode master warp, making the actual CUDA block size 64 + 32 = 96. However, looking at the SASS, the kernel uses SR_TID.X and barriers, and the OpenMP runtime on clang for sm_86 in generic mode launches blockDim = threads + warp_size = 64 + 32 = 96. But standard behavior for recent clang is to use SPMD mode when possible; examining the SASS prologue shows initialization patterns (STS to shared memory offsets 0x8, 0xc, 0x10) consistent with generic mode with a master warp. So blockSz = [96, 1, 1].
metrics_explanations.fp32_flop_explanation:
Looking at the SASS, the FP32 operations are: (1) I2F.RP (integer to float conversion, counted as FP32) - appears twice in the kernel (once at 0x03b0 and once at 0x0c90), used for the integer division emulation. (2) MUFU.RCP (reciprocal, FP32) - appears twice (0x03c0 and 0x0ca0). (3) F2I.FTZ (float to int, counted as FP32) - appears twice (0x03e0 and 0x0cc0). (4) I2FP.F32.U32 at 0x0820 - one FP32 conversion. (5) FSEL instructions at 0x0840, 0x0e70, 0x0eb0, 0x0ed0 - these are conditional selects on floats, which count as FP32 ops.

The kernel implements an in-place matrix transposition. With default params: A=197 (m), B=divceil(35588,32)=1113 (tiled_n), b=32 (s), m_val = A*B-1 = 219260. The kernel processes permutation cycles. Each "work item" fetched from h_head goes through the cycle detection and data movement. The total number of work items fetched equals m_val = 219260 (each element index 0..219260 is fetched once via atomic increment of h_head).

For each work item fetched, the initial division code executes (I2F.RP + MUFU.RCP + F2I = 3 FP32 ops). For items that are fixed points (next_in_cycle == lmem[1]), only these 3 FP32 ops execute. For non-fixed-point items, additional FP32 ops occur in the loop body: I2FP.F32.U32 (1), FSEL (1) on first iteration setup, then per inner loop iteration: division code (3 FP32: I2F.RP + MUFU.RCP + F2I) + FSEL x3 (3 FP32) = 6 FP32 per inner iteration.

Estimating the total is complex due to the permutation cycle structure. The number of fixed points is relatively small. The total inner loop iterations across all cycles equals approximately m_val (each non-fixed element is visited once as next_in_cycle). With 16 blocks × 64 worker threads, all threads in a block execute the same FP32 path (no per-thread divergence on FP32 ops since the division and FSEL are executed by all threads uniformly or conditionally).

Actually, looking more carefully: the division code runs once per outer while-loop iteration per thread (all 64 worker threads execute it). The FSEL and I2FP run per thread too. So for ~219260 work items, each processed by one team's worth of 64 threads: total FP32 ≈ 219260 × (3 for initial div) + inner_iterations × (6 for loop div+FSEL) all multiplied by 64 threads. But this is extremely large. Let me reconsider - the division is integer division emulated via FP32, and it's per-team not per-thread for the index computation. Looking at SASS, the division result goes into shared memory (lmem), so all threads compute it redundantly. Each of the 219260 items is processed by exactly one team. With 16 teams, each team processes ~219260/16 ≈ 13704 items. Per item: 3 FP32 ops (initial div). For non-fixed items, inner loop adds ~6 FP32 per iteration. Rough estimate: ~219260 items total, ~219260 inner iterations total, each executed by 64 threads: FP32 ≈ 219260 × 3 × 64 + 219260 × 6 × 64 ≈ 219260 × 9 × 64 ≈ 126,294,240. But many items are fixed points. Conservatively estimating ~125,000,000.

prediction.blockSz_explanation: The kernel uses `thread_limit(threads)` where threads = p.n_gpu_threads = 64. prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Looking at the SASS, the FP32 operations are: (1) I2F.RP (integer to float conversion, counted as FP32) appears twice in the kernel - once in the initial path and once in the loop body. (2) MUFU.RCP (reciprocal, FP32) appears twice. (3) FSEL instructions appear 4 times in the loop body (these are FP32 select/conditional move operations, which count as FP32). (4) I2F.U32 appears once. (5) HFMA2.MMA appears in the loop for constant materialization (counted as FP16, not FP32). The division algorithm uses I2F.RP + MUFU.RCP + F2I for integer division emulation. The FSEL instructions are conditional moves on floats. The key question is how many iterations the main while loop and inner for loop execute. With m = A*B - 1 = 197*1113 - 1 = 219260, the kernel processes elements 0 to 219260. Each team dynamically fetches work items. With 16 teams, each processes roughly 219261/16 ≈ 13704 items. For each item, there's the initial division (I2F.RP + MUFU.RCP = 2 FP32 ops), and some items enter the inner loop with another division (2 more FP32 ops) plus FSEL ops. However, many items are "fixed points" (next_in_cycle == lmem[1]) and skip quickly. The total number of non-fixed-point elements and cycle iterations is complex. Across all 16 teams × 64 active threads: each thread executes the I2F.RP and MUFU.RCP for the outer division. The FSEL and I2F.U32 are per-thread in the loop. Given the complexity, I'll estimate based on the structure: ~219261 outer iterations across all teams, each with 2 FP32 ops (I2F.RP, MUFU.RCP) per thread that executes them (only 1 thread per warp effectively does the division for the index, but actually all threads compute it). prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: In the SASS, there is one HFMA2.MMA instruction at address 0x08b0 that materializes a constant (0x2384185791015625e-07 which is 4 bytes = 0x34000000, used as a scaling factor of 4.0 for address computation). It executes once per inner loop iteration per thread. The inner loop processes cycle permutations. Estimating the total inner loop iterations across all teams and threads: with ~219261 work items distributed across 16 teams, and many being non-trivial cycles, the inner loop body executes for each step in each cycle. The total cycle steps across all elements equals roughly the number of non-fixed-point elements (~219261 minus fixed points). Each execution involves 64 threads, each executing 1 HFMA2 = 4 FP16 FLOPs. Estimating ~200,000 inner iterations total across all teams, with 64 threads each: 200000 * 64 * 4 = 51,200,000. This is a rough estimate given the data-dependent nature.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: The kernel operates on h_in_out (FP=float, 4 bytes) and h_finished (int, 4 bytes) and h_head (int, 4 bytes). Parameters: m=197, n=35588, s=32, tiled_n = divceil(35588,32) = 1113. in_size = 197 * 1113 * 32 = 7,015,488 floats = 28,061,952 bytes. finished_size = 197 * 1113 = 219,261 ints = 877,044 bytes. The kernel performs an in-place matrix transposition by cycling through permutation cycles. Each element is read and written once (approximately). The total data footprint is: h_in_out: ~28 MB read + h_finished: ~0.88 MB read + h_head: negligible. The L2 cache is 40 MB, so the entire working set (~29 MB) fits in L2. However, the data must first be loaded from DRAM into L2 on first access (compulsory misses). The h_in_out array was transferred to device via `omp target update to`, so it's already in device memory. On first kernel access, data comes from DRAM to L2. Since the access pattern is essentially random (permutation cycles), most of the ~28 MB of h_in_out will be read from DRAM. Similarly, h_finished (~0.88 MB) will be read. Total DRAM reads ≈ 28,061,952 + 877,044 + 4 ≈ 28,939,000 bytes.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes to h_in_out (transposed data), h_finished (marking completed elements), and h_head (atomic counter). The unique write footprint: h_in_out ≈ 28 MB (most elements written once), h_finished ≈ 0.88 MB (each element set to 1), h_head ≈ 4 bytes. Total unique write footprint ≈ 29 MB. Since the L2 cache is 40 MB and the total read+write working set is about 29 + 29 = 58 MB (though reads and writes overlap on the same addresses for h_in_out), the write footprint alone (~29 MB) fits in L2. However, since reads also compete for L2 space and the combined unique footprint of h_in_out (28 MB, both read and written) + h_finished (0.88 MB, both read and written) ≈ 29 MB total unique addresses, this fits within the 40 MB L2. Since the L2 is write-back, dirty lines stay in L2 until eviction. With the working set fitting in L2, most writes won't reach DRAM during the kernel execution. Some evictions may occur due to set conflicts in the L2 with random access patterns, but the majority should stay cached. I estimate minimal DRAM writes, perhaps ~5-10% spillover due to associativity conflicts with random access patterns: ~3 MB.

prediction.blockSz_explanation: The kernel uses `thread_limit(threads)` where threads = p.n_gpu_threads = 64. Given the LLVM OpenMP runtime behavior, the block size is typically 128 (next power of 2 or rounded) or 96. prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: Each super‑element (tile) contains 32 float values (128 B). The algorithm loads each tile once as source and once again as a backup during the permutation cycle, giving ~2 × 128 B = 256 B of FP reads per tile. Adding the int flag (4 B) and the atomic head read (4 B) yields ~264 B per tile. With 219,261 tiles (m=197, tiled_n=ceil(35588/32)=1113) the estimated DRAM reads are 219,261 × 256 ≈ 56 MB (rounded to 56,200,000 B).
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Each tile is written once (32 floats = 128 B) plus an int flag write (4 B) and the atomic head write (4 B), ≈136 B per tile. Multiplying by 219,261 tiles gives ≈29.8 MB; rounding to 28 MB acknowledges that some writes may hit L2 cache and not immediately reach DRAM.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The first target-kernel invocation is the first execution of the `#pragma omp target teams num_teams(blocks) thread_limit(threads)` region inside the rep loop. With no command-line arguments, `blocks=16` and `threads=64` from the `Params` defaults, so the defensible OpenMP offload estimate is 16 teams with thread_limit 64, mapped here to CUDA grid x-dimension 16 and block x-dimension 64.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: `thread_limit(threads)` constrains each OpenMP team to 64 threads on the first invocation because the default `n_gpu_threads` is 64. I assume the LLVM OpenMP GPU runtime honors this as a 1-D CUDA block of 64 threads for this kernel.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: `FP` is `float` because `DOUBLE_PRECISION` is not defined. Per work item processed by a team, the code computes `next_in_cycle = (x*A) - m*(x/B)` once before the inner loop and once at the end of each inner-loop iteration; over the permutation this is 2 integer muls + 1 integer div + 1 integer mul + 1 integer sub per evaluation, but those are integer, not FP, so the only floating-point arithmetic in the source is `data4 = omp_get_num_threads()` converted to float once for threads with `tid+3*num_threads < b`; with `b=32` and `num_threads=64` that condition is never true, so no FP32 arithmetic executes. Source-only analysis therefore gives zero FP32 FLOPs for the first invocation, noting hidden runtime/helper arithmetic is ignored without SASS.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: `FP` is not double in this build and the kernel source contains no double-precision arithmetic. Therefore the first invocation executes no FP64 FLOPs by source analysis.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The program uses `float`/`int` only and there are no half-precision variables or operations in the kernel source. Without SASS evidence of compiler-inserted packed FP16 instructions, the conservative estimate for the first invocation is zero FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: For the first invocation, the kernel permutes all `A*B = 197*1113 = 219261` tiles, each tile containing `b=32` floats, so the unique `h_in_out` read footprint is `219261*32*4 = 28,065,408` bytes. It also reads each `h_finished` flag once when checked/claimed (4 bytes each, 877,044 bytes total) and repeatedly accesses `h_head`, but `h_head` is only 4 bytes and stays resident after the first miss; since the total unique read footprint (~28.94 MB) fits within the 50 MB L2, DRAM reads are well approximated by this unique footprint loaded once.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes every `h_in_out` element exactly once during the permutation, giving a unique output footprint of `28,065,408` bytes, and writes every `h_finished` entry once plus updates `h_head` many times. However, the combined unique written footprint (~28.94 MB including `h_finished` and `h_head`) fits inside the 50 MB L2 cache on H100, so during this first invocation these dirty lines need not be evicted to DRAM; the best estimate for DRAM writes during the invocation is therefore zero.
